entries: African penguins forage in groups at sea and rely on calls to stay in contact. Using the acoustic mea-sures of 108 sea-surface calls, propagation correlations at seven distances and 139 paired playback experiments, we study what separates the three call types (flat, modulated, two-voice), how far each type carries, how penguins respond, and how noise changes the effective range.

For<s0> Problem 1</s0>, Kruskal–Wallis tests with Dunn comparisons, Mann–Whitney tests and PER-MANOVA show that only the peak frequency differs after Holm correction (⟦M0001⟧), with small effect sizes. A two-layer classifier makes the point: a structural rule (presence of a second funda-mental and of pulses) reaches 94.4% accuracy, whereas the continuous measures alone reach only 0.41–0.55. The call types are three ways of structuring a call, not three frequency bands. For<s1> Problem 2</s1>, the three correlations are averaged into a fidelity index and fitted with a signal-⟦M0002⟧ . Under the thresholds 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 the effective dis-to-noise curve tances of flat, modulated and two-voice calls are 155/225/245 m, 83/144/177 m and 41/85/107 m. Block bootstrap, between-sample ranges and alternative curves quantify the uncertainty. A gated response model fitted to the playbacks shows that a vocal reply requires a fidelity of at most 0.30, while approach requires about 0.49 (95% CI 0.32–0.58). For<s2> Problem 3</s2>, calls elicit a response in 64.7% of the experiments against 12.9% for the control sound (exact McNemar⟦M0003⟧). Whether penguins respond depends on context and group size, not on call type. A penalised multinomial model compares calls and control in one framework, and a mixture cure model shows that latency lengthens by a factor of 1.33 per 50 m while 35% of playbacks never elicit a visible response. For<s3> Problem 4</s3>, an effectiveness index combines tier-specific recognition probabilities with post-recognition behaviour. Contact radii are 155/225/245 m and recruitment radii 83/144/177 m. A 20% loss of correlation shortens the recruitment radius by 21–33%, and a 3 dB rise in noise removes 27–47% of the communication area. Recruitment is lost before contact, which leads to concrete recommendations on vessel noise in foraging areas.

The African penguin (<s0>Spheniscus demersus</s0>) breeds on the coasts of southern Africa and feeds

on pelagic fish in nearby waters. Its population has been falling by about 8% per year and the species is now assessed as Critically Endangered [3]. At sea the birds often forage in groups, and group foraging raises their catch rate [4]. Waves, glare and low visibility limit visual signals, so calls are the likely means by which penguins at the surface stay in contact and gather into groups.
Thiebault et al. [1, 2] recorded sea-surface calls, played calls and a control sound back to penguins at sea, and measured how the calls degrade with distance. The problem is built on these data.
•<s0> Problem 1.</s0> Describe and visualise the acoustic measures of the three call types (flat, modulated
“mod”, two-voice “tv”), test their differences with at least two non-parametric tests, find the main factors, build a classifier, and discuss function and transmission robustness.

•<s0> Problem 2.</s0> Combine the spectrogram, amplitude-spectrum and envelope correlations into a fidelity index, model its degradation with distance for each call type, design tiered recognition thresholds, and estimate effective communication distances with uncertainty and sensitivity analysis.

•<s0> Problem 3.</s0> Compare responses to calls and to the control sound; relate responses to context, call type, distance and group size; analyse the distribution of response combinations in a unified framework; model response intensity and latency; and give predictions at 50, 100 and 150 m.

•<s0> Problem 4.</s0> Build an index of communication effectiveness, estimate effective radii or ex-pected numbers of responders, analyse noise scenarios, and give recommendations for future experiments and for conservation.
Figure 1 shows how the three data sets feed the four problems. One thread runs through the

paper. The call types differ in structure rather than in frequency band; structure decides how far a call carries; a vocal reply still occurs where the signal is heavily degraded, whereas approach occurs only where the call is still recognisable; hence added noise removes recruitment before it removes contact. Each step of this thread is tested on the data.

The acoustic file (Data01) holds 108 calls: 44 flat, 40 mod and 24 tv. The second fundamental
F02 exists only for tv calls, and the pulse rate is missing for all flat calls. These gaps are structural
(a call without two voices has no second fundamental), so we do not impute them; the two columns are compared only where they exist and enter the classifier as presence indicators.
The playback file (Data02) holds 278 rows, i.e. 139 experiments with one call playback and

one control playback each. This is a paired design, and all comparisons between call and control respect the pairing. Nine latencies were recorded although the corresponding response flag was 0; we follow the flag and set them to missing. We verified that the overall flag equals “at least one of the three behaviours” and that the relative number of calls equals max(calls after⟦M0001⟧ calls before⟦M0002⟧ Head-up and approach durations are capped at 60 s (4 and 7 records), which gives the length of the observation window. The propagation files (Data03–11) give, for each call type and each of the three measures, 300 rows of correlations at 4–256 m. Missing values come in runs of 10 rows at identical positions in the three files of a call type, so one row is one pair of recordings and the three correlations can be combined row by row. The three blocks of 100 rows differ visibly (for mod at 128 m the block means are 0.51, 0.51 and 0.68); the rows are therefore not independent, and interval estimates use block resampling [13].

The structural rule classifies 102 of 108 calls correctly; the six errors are mod calls without

a pulse-rate record. The continuous measures do far worse. Logistic regression and LDA are no better than always guessing “flat”, and the random forest reaches 0.55 only after the harmonic ratio and the bandwidth are added; its recall for tv is 0.25. The three call types are therefore three ways

of structuring a call (plain tone, pulsed, two voices) that occupy the same band and have the same duration. Three rankings of the continuous measures (effect size⟦M0001⟧, largest standardised logistic coeffi-cient, permutation importance of the random forest on test folds) agree that the peak frequency and F01 come first. The decisive factors, however, are the two structural features.
A first look at the other two data sets already separates the types. At 128 m the spectrogram

correlation is 0.41 for flat, 0.62 for mod and 0.74 for tv. In the playbacks, flat calls mostly elicit head-up plus vocal reply (31%) and rarely approach (8%); tv calls elicit the largest share of vocal-only replies (31%); mod calls the largest share of responses with approach (24%). The type of the first reply is unrelated to the type played (⟦M0001⟧ ⟦M0002⟧). Two working hypotheses follow: the pulsed and two-voice structures transmit better, and the types differ in the form of the response they elicit. Problem 2 confirms the first; Problems 3 and 4 show that the second is largely a consequence of transmission. The key indicators carried forward are the presence of F02 (two-voice structure, reflected in the spectrogram correlation), the presence of pulses or beats (envelope correlation), the harmonic position of the peak frequency (amplitude-spectrum correlation) and F01. They enter Problem 3 through the call-type factor and through the predicted fidelity of each playback.

Whether penguins respond depends on context and group size (Table 9): the odds are 4.75 times higher when searching, and fall to 0.47 for each unit of ln⟦M0001⟧. Call type has no effect on responding. Distance does not affect whether penguins respond but changes how they respond: per 50 m the odds of head-up fall to 0.51 and those of approach to 0.55, while vocal replies do not decline. For approach, mod calls have 3.28 times the odds of flat calls. Variance inflation factors are at most 2.1. The group-size effect has a further implication (Figure 7, right). If each bird responded indepen-dently with a fixed probability, larger groups would respond more often; the opposite is observed. Inverting the independence formula gives 0.3–1.5 expected responders in every size class: about one bird responds per playback, whatever the group size.

Figure 9 shows the Kaplan–Meier curves of the first response. They flatten within 10 s: 98.9%

of the responses occur in the first 10 s, the slowest at 17.6 s, and 35.3% of the call playbacks never elicit a response. This is what “no response does not mean the stimulus was not perceived” looks like in the data: no response is a separate outcome, not a response that has not yet happened. An ordinary survival model treats it as censoring and so assumes that every group would respond if observed long enough, which is wrong here. Four conclusions follow. (i) Flat calls are the most fragile: a 20% loss of correlation shortens

their recruitment radius by 33%, against 25% and 21% for mod and tv. (ii) Recruitment is lost before contact: the same loss shortens the contact radius by only 12–22%, and raising the threshold to 0.7 shortens the recruitment radius by 39–51% (two thirds to three quarters of the area) while the probability of any response within 150 m is unchanged. (iii) At 100 m the probability of approach falls from 0.23 to 0.06 for mod and from 0.18 to 0.10 for tv when the threshold rises to 0.7 (Table 18).

(iv) Tv calls are the most stable under moderate scenarios, but their near-field level is only 0.745: with⟦M0001⟧ and a further 10% loss the mean curve no longer reaches the threshold and⟦M0002⟧ drops to zero, while the effective-area radius is still 61 m. Both radii should be reported. Under M3 a rise of the ambient noise level by ∆⟦M0003⟧ dB lowers the signal-to-noise ratio by the same amount and rescales the characteristic distance,

so every threshold distance shrinks by the same factor. A 3 dB rise multiplies the radii of flat, mod and tv by 0.73, 0.80 and 0.86 and removes 47%, 36% and 27% of the communication area; 6 dB removes 72%, 60% and 46%. This links the abstract scenarios to the decibel quantities used in the management of vessel noise [20].
Each recommendation answers a limitation visible in the data.
